name: Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
question: Should a person approve this before it happens?
summary: The agent works on its own until it reaches an action that is risky, irreversible or above a limit, and then pauses. Its state is saved, a person approves, edits or rejects the proposed action, and the run resumes from exactly where it stopped, even hours later. Frameworks call the pause an interrupt or an approval; the design work is choosing which steps pause and what the reviewer sees.
useCases: Actions that move money, change records or contact customers
Steps above a policy limit, such as refunds over ₹10,000
Early rollout, while you still measure how often the agent is wrong

items.detail: a pause point before a tool call or inside a step, chosen by a rule
always, never, or a function of the arguments, such as amount or customer type
the paused run is stored (a checkpointer or serialised run state) so it can wait hours
what the reviewer sees: the action, its arguments, the reason and the evidence
approve, edit the arguments, or reject with a note the agent reads
continue from the saved point with the decision, and log who decided

steps: List the actions and mark which are irreversible or above a limit
Put the approval rule in code on the tool or step, not in the prompt
Save the paused run durably and send the reviewer a short card with the evidence
Resume with the decision, and log who approved what and when
pitfalls: Pausing on every step trains reviewers to approve without reading
Side effects placed before the pause run again when the step restarts
A paused run kept only in memory is lost on the next deploy or restart
remember: Pause before what you cannot undo. Save the state, show the evidence, resume cleanly.
caption: Illustrative: 1,000 refund requests a day at KhataPay, a fictional wallet, with a ₹10,000 approval limit.

comparison.scope: Your code pauses; a person decides
comparison.needs: Medium: saved state and a review screen

code.text: from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver   # use Postgres in production
LIMIT = 10_000   # rupees: the rule lives in code, not in the prompt
ticket: str; plan: dict; note: str
for name, fn in [("decide", decide), ("approve", approve), ("pay", pay), ("explain", explain)]:
out = app.invoke({"ticket": "T-7731"}, cfg)   # returns with out["__interrupt__"]

steps.title: Put the rule in code
steps.text: The approval limit is a constant in code: ₹10,000. Refunds at or below it go straight to payment. The prompt never decides whether a person is needed, so a clever customer message cannot talk its way past the check.

steps.title: Propose, don't act
steps.text: The decide step only proposes: refund ₹25,000 on ticket T-7731, with a reason and the evidence it used. Proposing and acting are separate steps, so a check can sit between them.

steps.title: Pause and save the state
steps.text: The amount is above the limit, so interrupt() pauses the run. The checkpointer saves the whole state under the thread id T-7731, and invoke returns at once. Nothing waits in memory.

steps.title: Show the reviewer the evidence
steps.text: The value passed to interrupt() is what the caller receives in __interrupt__: the action, amount, reason and evidence. Your review screen turns it into a card, so the reviewer judges facts, not a bare yes or no.

steps.title: Resume with the decision
steps.text: Hours later the reviewer approves, edits the amount or rejects with a note. Command(resume=…) continues the same thread, and the decision becomes the return value of interrupt(). The approve step restarts from its first line, so nothing before the pause may have side effects.

steps.title: Act once, after approval
steps.text: Only the pay step touches money, and it runs after the decision. The idempotency key tied to the ticket means a retried payment call cannot refund twice.

pros: Irreversible actions get a human decision without giving up automation
A limit keeps reviews to the few cases that matter
Every decision is logged: who, what, when and why
Reviewers can correct an argument instead of restarting the run
cons: Paused cases wait minutes or hours for a person
Needs durable state, a review screen and reviewers on shift
Too many pauses turn approval into a reflex
Resumed steps can repeat side effects if built carelessly
avoidWhen: Every action is cheap and reversible (log it and review samples afterwards)
Decisions must be made in seconds with nobody available (use automatic guardrails and hard limits)

playgroundGuide.scenario: KhataPay's refund agent handles 1,000 requests a day and gets 3% of them wrong: 30 refunds worth ₹6,00,000, mostly the larger ones. You decide which refunds pause for a person, what the reviewer sees, how many reviewers are on shift and where paused runs are kept.
controls: Pick the approval limit: every refund, a rupee amount, or no checkpoint at all.
Choose what the reviewer sees, and drag the slider to set how many reviewers are on shift.
Choose whether paused runs live in server memory or in a database, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Paused for review
outputs.meaning: How many of the 1,000 daily refunds stop for a person, and how many of the 30 wrong ones are among them.

outputs.name: Wrong refunds stopped
outputs.meaning: The share and rupee value of wrong refunds that reviewers catch before payout.

outputs.name: Reviews per reviewer
outputs.meaning: Daily reviews for each person. Past 150, reviewers start approving on autopilot.

outputs.name: Median wait
outputs.meaning: How long a paused customer waits for a decision, or how many cases are left unreviewed.

outputs.name: Paused runs lost
outputs.meaning: Runs that vanish at the daily deploy because their state was only in memory.

presets.name: Approve everything, bare card
presets.expect: 1,000 reviews, 500 each: reviewers approve on autopilot, only ₹1,44,000 stopped, and 250 paused runs lost at the deploy.

presets.name: Limit ₹10,000, evidence, database
presets.expect: 90 reviews, 45 each, 16-minute wait: ₹4,27,500 stopped (71%), nothing lost.

presets.name: No checkpoint
presets.expect: No reviews and no waiting, and all ₹6,00,000 of wrong refunds are paid out.

missions.text: Stop at least 75% of the wrong money while keeping every reviewer at 150 cases a day or fewer.
missions.hint: Show the evidence and try a ₹5,000 limit with 2 reviewers, or ₹2,000 with 3.

missions.text: Show how pausing every refund makes reviewers miss mistakes.
missions.hint: Choose every refund and keep 1 or 2 reviewers: the catch rate falls below half.

missions.text: Keep paused runs through the daily deploy while stopping at least 70% of the wrong money.
missions.hint: Store paused runs in a database and use a ₹10,000 or lower limit with evidence.

tools.best: interrupt() inside a step saves the state with a checkpointer; Command(resume=…) continues the same thread.
pros: Resume hours later from a durable checkpoint
Approve, edit or reject in one pattern
cons: The step restarts on resume, so code before the pause must be safe to repeat
Needs a checkpointer and thread ids

practice.scenario: KhataPay, a fictional wallet, lets an agent resolve refund tickets. Refunds up to ₹10,000 are paid automatically. Anything larger pauses: the run is saved, a reviewer sees the amount, the reason and the statement lines the agent relied on, and approves, edits or rejects. About 9% of refunds pause, reviewers stop most of the costly mistakes, and every decision is logged with the reviewer's name.

industries.use: Refunds, reversals and chargebacks above a limit wait for an operations reviewer
Loan offers outside policy, or a waiver of charges, pause for a credit officer
A drafted prescription change or discharge note waits for a doctor to sign

practice.analogy: A bank teller and a branch manager. The teller handles routine withdrawals; anything above a limit needs the manager's signature before cash leaves the counter, and the slip records who signed.

library.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
library.what: Mark a tool with needs_approval and the run pauses before it executes; the paused run becomes a RunState you can approve, reject, store and resume.

practice.note: The refund body is a stub. For waits of hours, store state.to_json() and load it later with RunState.from_json(agent, stored). Check the SDK docs for your version.

samples.code:
import asyncio
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool

async def over_limit(_ctx, params, _call_id) -> bool:
    return params["amount"] > 10_000          # the rule lives in code

@function_tool(needs_approval=over_limit)
async def issue_refund(ticket_id: str, amount: int) -> str:
    """Refund a customer to the original payment method."""
    return f"refunded ₹{amount} for {ticket_id}"

agent = Agent(name="Refunds",
              instructions="Resolve refund tickets. Check the facts, then use issue_refund.",
              tools=[issue_refund])

async def main():
    result = await Runner.run(agent, "Ticket T-7731: rent of ₹25,000 was debited twice.")
    if result.interruptions:                   # paused before the refund ran
        state = result.to_state()
        for item in result.interruptions:
            print("Needs approval:", item.name, item.arguments)
            state.approve(item)                # or state.reject(item)
        result = await Runner.run(agent, state)
    print(result.final_output)

asyncio.run(main())

numericDrill.question: KhataPay pauses refunds above ₹10,000 for a person. 9% of its 1,000 daily refunds are above the limit, and a careful review takes 2 minutes. How many reviewer-hours a day does that need?
numericDrill.answer: 90 reviews × 2 minutes = 180 minutes = 3 hours a day. Pausing every refund would need 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 minutes, over 33 hours.

interview.question: How do you decide which agent actions need human approval?
interview.answer: Start from impact: actions that move money, change records, contact customers or cannot be undone. Set a rule in code, often a limit on the amount or a customer type, and measure how often the agent is wrong in each band. Pause where errors are costly and frequent enough, and keep the pause rate low enough that reviewers read each case.

interview.question: What goes wrong when an approval step is added naively?
interview.answer: Pausing everything makes reviewers approve on autopilot. Keeping paused runs in memory loses them on a restart. Side effects placed before the pause repeat when the step resumes. Showing only "approve?" gives reviewers nothing to judge. Store state durably, show evidence, keep side effects after the decision and log who decided.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for approval on every step
mistakes.fix: Pause only above a limit or for irreversible actions, and track reviewer load

mistakes.mistake: Keeping paused runs in server memory
mistakes.fix: Save them with a durable checkpointer or serialised run state

quiz.question: A wallet’s refund agent is right 97% of the time. Refunds above ₹10,000 are 9% of volume but most of the money lost to mistakes. Where should a human checkpoint go?
options: After refunds are paid, in a weekly audit only
quiz.explanation: Pause where errors are costly: the high-value band holds most of the risk at a fraction of the volume.

quiz.question: An NBFC asks the model, in its system prompt, to "ask a human before approving loans over ₹5 lakh". A customer writes a message that talks the model out of asking. What was the design flaw?
options: The approval rule lived in the prompt instead of in code
quiz.explanation: Rules that must hold belong in code on the tool or step, where no message can argue with them.

quiz.question: A claims agent pauses for approval, but the paused runs are held in server memory. What happens at the nightly deploy?
options: Paused runs are lost and those customers never get an answer
quiz.explanation: State that must survive hours of waiting needs a durable checkpointer or serialised run state.

quiz.question: Reviewers at a payments company approve 600 refund cards a day each, and almost never reject one. What is the most likely problem?
options: Approval on autopilot: too many pauses for careful review
quiz.explanation: When reviewers are overloaded, approval becomes automatic. Raise the limit or add evidence and staff.

quiz.question: A marketplace’s reviewer card says only "Approve refund? Yes / No". What should be added first?
options: The amount, the reason and the evidence the agent used
The customer’s full order history for five years
quiz.explanation: Reviewers can only judge what they see; the action, reason and evidence make the decision checkable.

quiz.question: In LangGraph, a node sends an SMS "refund on its way" and then calls interrupt(). After the reviewer approves, the customer gets the SMS twice. Why?
options: On resume the node restarts from its first line, so the SMS runs again
quiz.explanation: Code before interrupt() re-runs on resume. Side effects belong after the decision.

quiz.question: A reviewer spots that a proposed ₹48,000 refund should be ₹4,800. What should the checkpoint allow?
options: Editing the amount, then resuming with the corrected action
Restarting the whole run from the customer’s message
Asking the agent to try again until it gets ₹4,800
quiz.explanation: An edit decision fixes the argument and resumes, without losing the work already done.

quiz.question: An approved order is sent to the exchange, times out, and the agent retries. What prevents a duplicate order?
options: An idempotency key tied to the approved action
quiz.explanation: Approval decides whether to act; an idempotency key makes sure the action happens once.

quiz.question: Which actions are good candidates for a human checkpoint in a lending agent? Select all that apply.
options: Waiving a late-payment charge above a limit
Offering a loan outside the policy grid
quiz.explanation: Pause on actions that change money or policy outcomes; reading and formatting are safe to automate.

quiz.question: A hospital agent drafts discharge summaries. Doctors must sign each one. Which design fits?
options: Automatic sending with a weekly sample review
A checkpoint on every summary, with the draft and source notes on the card
A checkpoint only on long summaries
quiz.explanation: When every item legally needs a signature, every item pauses, and the card must make review fast.

quiz.question: With OpenAI’s Agents SDK, how do you make one tool pause for approval only when the amount is over ₹10,000?
options: Put the rule in the agent instructions
Set needs_approval to a function that checks the amount
Use a smaller model for large amounts
quiz.explanation: needs_approval accepts a function of the call’s arguments, so the rule stays in code.

quiz.question: A benefits agent pauses decisions for an officer. Auditors ask who approved a payment six months ago. What should exist?
options: The model’s memory of the conversation
A log of each decision: who, what, when and the evidence shown
quiz.explanation: Checkpoints are only auditable if every decision and its evidence are recorded.

quiz.question: Paused runs for number porting wait up to three days for a regulator’s response. Which tool suits that wait best?
options: A durable workflow engine such as Temporal, or a durable checkpointer
A cron job that restarts the agent
quiz.explanation: Long waits need state that survives restarts and deploys.

quiz.question: Moving the refund approval limit from ₹10,000 down to ₹2,000 quadruples the pauses. What should the team watch?
options: Only the number of wrong refunds stopped
Reviewer load and the approval rate, as signs of reviewing on autopilot
quiz.explanation: More pauses catch more only while reviewers still read each case; watch load and near-100% approval rates.

quiz.question: A paused refund resumes after approval. Which should run after the decision, not before the pause? Select all that apply.
options: Building the review card from the evidence
Writing the refund to the ledger
quiz.explanation: Anything that changes the world waits for the decision; preparing the card is read-only.

quiz.question: A reviewer rejects a claim payout with the note "policy lapsed in May". What should the agent do next?
options: Read the note and explain the rejection to the customer
Escalate to another reviewer until someone approves
quiz.explanation: A rejection note is input the agent acts on; shopping for an approval defeats the checkpoint.

quiz.question: An agent can cancel orders, which is easy to reverse within an hour. Should every cancellation pause for a person?
options: No: automate it, log it and review a sample afterwards
quiz.explanation: Cheap, reversible actions are better handled by logging and sampling than by pausing.

quiz.question: A LangGraph agent pauses but the review screen cannot find the run to resume. What was probably missing?
options: A checkpointer and a stable thread id for the run
quiz.explanation: Resuming needs the saved state and the thread id that identifies it.

quiz.question: Three weeks after launch, reviewers approve 99.6% of paused refunds and the agent’s errors in that band are near zero. What could the team consider?
options: Raising the limit or sampling reviews, while keeping the log
quiz.explanation: Checkpoints should follow measured risk; when a band proves safe, reduce pauses but keep the record.

quiz.question: Which make a review card faster and more reliable to judge? Select all that apply.
options: The proposed action and its arguments
The evidence the agent relied on
The model’s full raw token stream
A short reason in plain words
quiz.explanation: Show the action, reason and evidence; raw model output slows reviewers without helping them decide.
